entries.title: 2025 changes: 'assessment or assurance', value-chain deferral, green credits
entries.officialText: Paraphrase (full text not opened): the Board decided to revise provisions on ESG disclosures for value chain, provide an option to undertake 'assessment' or 'assurance' for BRSR Core and ESG disclosures for value chain, and introduce disclosure on green credits.
entries.whatToReport: Choose third-party assessment (against Industry Standards Forum standards) or assurance for BRSR Core; glide path unchanged (top 500 in FY2025-26, top 1,000 in FY2026-27). Value-chain disclosures deferred and made voluntary (top 250 from FY2025-26; assessment/assurance voluntary from FY2026-27). New Principle 6 Leadership Indicator 8 on green credits. Provider must have no conflict of interest (no consulting or other non-assessment services to the group).
entries.whyNeeded: SEBI swapped 'reasonable assurance' for 'assessment or assurance' so that firms other than auditors can check the Core numbers, but the evidence standard did not soften: the assessor still needs traceable source data. The independence rule means the firm that checks the BRSR cannot also be the ESG consultant. These changes came from the May 2024 Expert Committee report, the 18 Dec 2024 Board decision and the 28 Mar 2025 circular.
evidence: Assessment/assurance engagement terms naming the ISF standard or assurance standard used

entries.title: ESG disclosures for the value chain - what a listed company collects from partners
entries.officialText: Listed entities shall report the KPIs in the BRSR Core for their value chain to the extent it is attributable to their business with that value chain partner. Such reporting may be segregated for upstream and downstream partners or can be reported on an aggregate basis.
entries.whatToReport: Current rule (from 28 Mar 2025): top 250 listed entities, voluntary from FY2025-26; value chain = upstream and downstream partners individually 2% or more of purchases / sales by value; disclosure may be limited to partners covering 75% of purchases / sales; disclose the % of purchases and sales covered; assessment or assurance voluntary from FY2026-27. Original 2023 rule (superseded): top partners cumulatively 75% of purchases / sales, comply-or-explain from FY2024-25, limited assurance from FY2025-26. Scope, assumptions and estimates must be disclosed.
entries.unit: BRSR Core units (tCO2e, kL, GJ, t, %, days) pro-rated to the business done with the listed entity
entries.whyNeeded: For a top-250 company such as Asian Paints this decides which suppliers (for example titanium dioxide, resins and monomers, solvents, packaging) and which large customers or distributors are asked for BRSR Core data, pro-rated to their business with the listed company. Partners answer the same questions esgOS asks its own plants (fuel, electricity, water, waste, safety), so their plant data must be just as traceable. Bikaji, unless it enters the top 250, has no value-chain disclosure duty but may receive data requests as a supplier.
evidence: Purchase and sales ledger analysis identifying partners at or above 2% and the cumulative % covered
Partner data templates with the allocation basis (e.g., share of partner revenue or volume)
Statement of scope, assumptions and estimates

entries.whyNeeded: Withdrawal must be split by source (borewell, municipal or industrial-estate supply, tanker, rainwater), so esgOS asks where water comes from and whether it is metered. Assessors want calibrated meter logs; estimates must be disclosed.

entries.officialText: Provide details of greenhouse gas emissions (Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions) & its intensity, in the following format: Total Scope 1 emissions (Break-up of the GHG into CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6, NF3, if available) ... Total Scope 2 emissions ... per rupee of turnover ...

core.parameter: Total Scope 1 emissions; Total Scope 2 emissions; GHG Emission Intensity (Scope 1+2)
core.measurement: Metric tonnes of CO2e. Scope 2 = consumption x emission factor (ISF: latest applicable CEA grid factor). Intensity = total Scope 1+2 (t) / revenue from operations adjusted for PPP, and per unit of physical output. The specified approach is a base methodology; any industry-specific adjustments or estimates must be disclosed (circular para 3.2).

entries.whyNeeded: Scope 1 comes from fuels burnt on site (boilers, thermic fluid heaters, DG sets, forklifts, owned vehicles), process emissions and refrigerant or SF6 leaks. Scope 2 comes from purchased electricity. Each figure is activity x factor: CEA grid factor for electricity, IPCC defaults or measured calorific values for fuels, AR5 or AR6 GWPs for refrigerants (state which). Biogenic CO2 from biomass is reported separately; its CH4 and N2O stay in Scope 1.
evidence: Emission-factor register with source and version

entries.ref: Corporate Standard (Revised Edition), Chapter 3 - Setting Organizational Boundaries
entries.title: Organisational boundary: equity share vs financial vs operational control
entries.officialText: Paraphrase: companies consolidate GHG emissions using either the equity share approach or a control approach (financial or operational). Under control, a company accounts for 100 percent of emissions from operations it controls; joint ventures under joint financial control are accounted on an equity-share basis.
entries.whatToReport: State the approach; apply it to all operations. Worked examples: 50% JV - equity share 50%; financial control 100% if you have financial control, 50% if joint financial control, 0% otherwise; operational control 100% if you operate it, else 0%. 74% subsidiary - equity share 74%; financial control 100%; operational control 100% if you operate it (normally yes), 0% if the partner operates it.
entries.whyNeeded: BRSR does not prescribe a GHG consolidation approach, so state it and keep it consistent with the Section A reporting boundary. Operational control is the most common choice for Indian manufacturers because it matches what plant teams can measure. A toll manufacturer or third-party-operated plant usually falls into Scope 3 rather than Scope 1 or 2. The GHG Protocol is currently revising Chapter 3, so watch for changes.
evidence: Entity / site list with ownership % and who operates each site

entries.ref: Corporate Standard, Chapter 4 - Setting Operational Boundaries
entries.title: Scope 1, 2 and 3 definitions and operational boundary
entries.officialText: Paraphrase: Scope 1 - direct GHG emissions from sources owned or controlled by the company; Scope 2 - emissions from the generation of purchased electricity (and heat, steam, cooling) consumed by the company; Scope 3 - all other indirect emissions in the value chain. Companies shall separately account for and report Scopes 1 and 2 at a minimum.
entries.whatToReport: Scope 1 categories: stationary combustion (boilers, thermic fluid heaters, DG), mobile combustion (owned vehicles, forklifts), process, fugitive (refrigerants, SF6 in switchgear, CO2 extinguishers). Scope 2: grid and purchased steam/heat/cooling.
entries.whyNeeded: The SEBI BRSR guidance uses these same definitions. Each esgOS site question maps to a Scope 1 source type (fuels, refrigerants) or to Scope 2 (electricity billing).

entries.ref: Corporate Standard, Chapter 5 - Tracking Emissions Over Time
entries.title: Base year and recalculation
entries.officialText: Companies shall choose and report a base year for which verifiable emissions data are available and specify their reasons for choosing that particular year.
entries.whatToReport: Base year; recalculation policy and significance threshold; recalculations for structural changes (acquisitions, divestments, outsourcing / insourcing) and methodology or factor changes.

entries.title: Location-based vs market-based Scope 2
entries.officialText: Paraphrase: companies with operations in markets providing product or supplier-specific data in the form of contractual instruments shall report scope 2 in two ways - location-based (grid-average factors) and market-based (contractual instruments) - 'dual reporting'.
entries.whatToReport: Location-based: kWh x CEA weighted-average grid factor. Market-based: kWh covered by qualifying instruments (RE certificates, I-RECs, green tariff, open-access / captive RE PPAs) at their factor; the rest at a residual mix, or the grid average if none is published (disclose).
entries.whyNeeded: BRSR asks for 'Total Scope 2' without naming a method, and the ISF standard (per secondary sources) points to the CEA grid factor. Report location-based Scope 2 in BRSR and add market-based where the company buys RE. India has no published residual-mix factor, so state what was used.

entries.title: R-22 and other non-Kyoto gases; biogenic CO2 from biomass
entries.officialText: Paraphrase: emissions of GHGs not covered by the Kyoto Protocol (e.g., CFCs, NOx) shall not be included in scope 1 but may be reported separately; direct CO2 emissions from the combustion of biomass shall not be included in scope 1 but reported separately.
entries.whatToReport: Report HCFC-22 (R-22) leaks separately (memo) from Scope 1; report biomass-combustion CO2 separately; keep biomass CH4 and N2O in Scope 1.
entries.whyNeeded: Old split ACs and chillers still run on R-22, an ozone-depleting HCFC, so its leaks are shown outside the Scope 1 total. Biomass briquettes in a snacks fryer heater make most of that heater's CO2 'biogenic', but its CH4 and N2O are still Scope 1. entries.officialText: Paraphrase of s.25 Water Act: no person shall, without the previous consent of the State Board, establish any industry, operation or process likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent into a stream, well, sewer or on land. Air Act s.21 requires consent to establish or operate an industrial plant in an air pollution control area.
entries.whatToReport: Valid CTE (before construction/expansion) and CTO (before and during operation) from the SPCB; renewal before expiry; compliance with conditions.
entries.whyNeeded: A CTO typically sets the permitted products and capacity, water use, effluent volume and discharge standards or a ZLD requirement, stack heights and emission limits, permitted fuels, monitoring frequency and validity; many states combine it with the hazardous-waste authorisation. These are the numbers BRSR Principle 6 reports against. Validity depends on the CPCB colour category: secondary sources cite 5 years for Red, 10 for Orange and 15 for Green, and state practice varies. CPCB revised the categories in 2025 (Red PI 80 or more, Orange 55-79, Green 25-54, White below 25, plus a new Blue category). White-category units are exempt from CTE/CTO and file a self-declaration, and projects with Environmental Clearance no longer need a separate CTE (secondary). Paints and food plants are usually Red or Orange depending on process; confirm the exact entry in the 2025 list.
evidence: CTE and CTO orders with conditions and validity

entries.ref: Environment (Protection) Rules 1986: Rule 14 (Environmental Statement, Form V); Schedule VI (General Standards)
entries.title: Environmental Statement (Form V) and general discharge standards
entries.officialText: Paraphrase of Rule 14: every person carrying on an industry, operation or process requiring consent under s.25 Water Act or s.21 Air Act, or authorisation under the hazardous waste rules, shall submit an environmental statement for the financial year ending 31 March in Form V to the State Board on or before 30 September.
entries.whatToReport: Annual Form V (water and raw-material consumption per unit of product, pollutants discharged, hazardous and solid wastes, conservation measures). Schedule VI inland-surface-water limits include oil and grease 10 mg/L, BOD 30 mg/L, COD 250 mg/L, TSS 100 mg/L unless the CTO or a sector standard says otherwise.
entries.whyNeeded: Form V is the closest statutory twin of BRSR Principle 6. Its water per unit of product, pollutant loads and waste quantities should match the BRSR figures, and assessors often cross-check the two. The oil-and-grease limit matters for snack plants, where washdown water carries frying oil.
evidence: Filed Form V for the year

entries.officialText: Paraphrase (CPCB FAQ): bulk consumers of electrical and electronic equipment listed in Schedule I shall ensure that e-waste generated by them is handed over only to a registered producer, refurbisher or recycler.

entries.ref: Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 as amended (EPR Guidelines notified 16 Feb 2022; amendments 2024 and 2026)
entries.title: Plastic packaging EPR for producers, importers and brand owners (PIBOs)
entries.officialText: Paraphrase: EPR guidelines stipulate mandatory targets for collection, recycling and end-of-life disposal of plastic packaging, use of recycled content, and (selective) reuse by brand owners; PIBOs must register on the CPCB centralised EPR portal.
entries.whatToReport: Registration on the CPCB EPR portal (CPCB if operating in more than two states/UTs, else SPCB); packaging placed on market by category (I rigid, II flexible, III multilayered, IV compostable); EPR obligations met with certificates; annual return (by 30 June per secondary sources); recycled-content and reuse obligations.
entries.whyNeeded: Paints (plastic buckets and pails, rigid Category I) and snacks (multilayer pouches, Category III or II) both put plastic packaging on the market and so carry EPR targets. This feeds BRSR P2 E3-E4 and the plastic waste line in P6 E9. Secondary sources give Category I recycling targets of 60% in 2025-26 rising to 80% from 2027-28, and Category I recycled content of 30% in 2025-26 rising to 60% from 2028-29. The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules 2026 (G.S.R. 237(E), 31 Mar 2026) formalise tradeable certificates and annual reporting of virgin and recycled plastic use (secondary); verify the current targets in the gazette.

entries.title: Chemical safety: MAH installations, on-site emergency plans

entries.ref: BRSR P6 E6 (VOC line); Air Act consent conditions
entries.title: VOC and solvent emissions at paint plants
entries.officialText: Volatile organic compounds (VOC) - one of the parameters in BRSR P6 Essential Indicator 6 'Please provide details of air emissions (other than GHG emissions) by the entity'.
entries.whatToReport: VOC emissions (state unit: t/yr preferred, or measured concentration); method (stack/ambient monitoring or solvent mass balance); share of solvent-based vs water-based production.
entries.whyNeeded: Solvent-borne paint, solvent storage, dispersion and filling are the main VOC sources. Water-based production emits far less. Published emission factors show solvent-borne paints with several times the VOC of water-borne paints (secondary). A solvent mass balance (purchased minus in product, recovered and in waste) is often more complete than spot stack readings. No CPCB VOC standard specific to paint manufacturing was confirmed in this session; use the plant's CTO conditions.
evidence: Solvent purchase, issue and recovery records

entries.officialText: Not applicable (method note).
entries.whatToReport: Equipment list with refrigerant type and charge; kg topped up per year; Scope 1 HFC emissions; R-22 separately; ammonia (R-717) systems noted (not a GHG).
entries.whyNeeded: Sweets and dairy-based products need cold rooms, often running R-404A, R-134a or older R-22, while large stores may use ammonia. A 10 kg R-404A recharge is about 47 tCO2e (AR6), which can rival a month of diesel use. esgOS therefore asks for refrigerant type and top-up logs. Ammonia and CO2 (R-744) systems have negligible GWP but carry safety duties.

entries.whyNeeded: Festive-season peaks bring large numbers of contract or seasonal packers. Year-end headcount (Section A Q20) can understate them, but the BRSR Core safety metrics (LTIFR including contract workforce), the wage indicators and smaller-town wages all need their person-hours and wages. ESI coverage rules treat seasonal factories differently, so confirm each site's status.

entries.title: Cleaning and washdown water at food plants
entries.officialText: Paraphrase: Schedule VI general standards set oil and grease at 10 mg/L for discharge to inland surface water (unless the CTO specifies otherwise).
entries.whatToReport: Water used for cleaning / CIP (metered or estimated), potato or raw-material washing; effluent volume; oil-and-grease removal; discharge destination.
entries.whyNeeded: In snack plants much of the water goes to cleaning fryers, floors and equipment and to washing raw materials. That water returns as oily effluent, which must pass an oil trap or ETP before discharge or reuse. Metering cleaning water separately lets the site show intensity improvements and gives assessors a clean water balance.
evidence: ETP log book and O&G test reports

products.why: What a site makes sets its NIC code and turnover share in the BRSR (Section A Q16-17), the physical-output unit used for every 'intensity per unit of output', which hazardous wastes and EPR obligations to expect, and which licences apply. The product list should match the CTO and, for food, the FSSAI licence.
evidence: CTO product list and consented capacity

sectorNotes.paints: Separate water-based vs solvent-based paints, resins/intermediates and putty/powders; this drives VOC, spent solvent and water-balance expectations.
sectorNotes.snacks: Separate fried namkeen, baked items, sweets (cold storage) and packaged products; product mix drives oil use, heat demand and packaging EPR.

output.why: Annual production with a unit is the denominator for the BRSR 'intensity in terms of physical output' lines (energy, water, emissions, waste). It lets reviewers and assessors spot outliers by checking per-tonne or per-kilolitre figures. It must reconcile with production reports and sit within consented or licensed capacity.

sectorNotes.paints: Use a consistent unit (kL or tonnes) across plants; state the density used for conversions.
sectorNotes.snacks: Report tonnes of finished product; keep the unit consistent across fried, baked and sweets lines.

continuity.why: Whether a site runs continuously, in batches or seasonally changes how monthly data should look, how gaps are estimated, and how many contract or seasonal workers come and go. That affects headcount (Section A Q20), person-hours for LTIFR and wages in smaller towns. It also helps assessors judge whether low months are real or missing data.

sectorNotes.snacks: Festive-season peaks are typical; capture peak contract/seasonal headcount and months.

boilers.why: Boilers and thermic fluid heaters are usually the largest Scope 1 source at a plant and a main stack emission source. Knowing they exist tells esgOS to collect fuel quantities (energy, Scope 1), stack monitoring (air emissions) and registration or inspection certificates.

sectorNotes.paints: Resin and intermediates plants commonly use thermic fluid heaters; decorative paint blending may need little process heat.
sectorNotes.snacks: Continuous fryers/roasters typically use thermic fluid heaters; steam boilers may serve cooking/cleaning.

boilerFuel.why: The fuel decides the emission factor and calorific value, whether the energy counts as renewable (biomass) or not (HSD, LDO, furnace oil, coal, PNG, LPG), and how CO2 is split (biomass CO2 is biogenic and reported outside Scope 1). The CTO usually names permitted fuels, so a fuel switch may need a consent amendment.
evidence: PNG bills showing SCM and GCV

sectorNotes.snacks: Biomass briquettes (renewable, biogenic CO2) and PNG are common; ask for briquette calorific value and moisture.

fuelQuantitySource.why: An assessor will rebuild the Scope 1 and energy numbers from source documents, so esgOS needs to know whether fuel is measured (flow meter, weighbridge, PNG meter) or derived (purchases plus or minus stock). Derived figures need opening and closing stock and a stated density for litre-to-tonne conversion.

waterSource.why: BRSR splits water withdrawal by source (surface, groundwater, third-party, seawater, others), and groundwater use needs a CGWA or state NOC with a permitted quantity. Sites in stressed areas also need site-level water reporting under Leadership Indicator 1.

sectorNotes.paints: Water is a product ingredient in water-based paint; record it as withdrawal and consumption.
sectorNotes.snacks: Raw-material washing and cleaning dominate; consider sub-metering cleaning water.

waterMetered.why: The BRSR Core water measurement approach expects calibrated meters, and the CGWA requires a digital flow meter with telemetry for groundwater abstraction under an NOC. Unmetered withdrawal becomes an estimate that must be disclosed and is a common assessment finding.

discharge.why: BRSR asks for water discharged by destination and treatment level and whether the site is ZLD. Both must match the CTO (which may require ZLD or set discharge standards) and the Environmental Statement. Discharge also closes the water balance: consumption = withdrawal - discharge.
evidence: ETP/STP log books and outlet meter

sectorNotes.paints: Many paint plants run ZLD and reuse wash water in the next water-based batch.
sectorNotes.snacks: Oily washdown effluent needs oil-and-grease removal (Schedule VI limit 10 mg/L for inland surface water unless the CTO says otherwise).

wasteStreams.why: Each stream must be placed in one of BRSR's eight waste categories (plastic, e-waste, bio-medical, C&D, battery, radioactive, other hazardous, other non-hazardous) and reconciled with the hazardous-waste authorisation and Form 4 return. The list also shows whether EPR, e-waste and solid-waste rules apply.

sectorNotes.paints: Expect paint sludge/process residues (Sch. I 21.1), spent solvent (21.2), ETP sludge, contaminated drums and liners, used oil.
sectorNotes.snacks: Expect used cooking oil, off-spec product, peels/food waste, packaging scrap, ETP sludge, used oil.

wasteDisposal.why: BRSR splits waste into recovered (recycled, re-used, other recovery such as co-processing) and disposed (incineration, landfill, other). Each hazardous consignment needs a Form 10 manifest and a receiver authorised for that waste.

refrigeration.why: Refrigeration and HVAC leaks are Scope 1 fugitive emissions, small in mass but large in CO2e. The refrigerant type decides whether a leak is in Scope 1 (HFCs such as R-134a, R-404A, R-410A, R-32) or reported separately (R-22, an ozone-depleting HCFC being phased out by 2030). Chillers and cold rooms also use significant electricity (Scope 2).
evidence: Equipment register with refrigerant type and charge (nameplates)

sectorNotes.paints: Process chillers and building HVAC are typical.
sectorNotes.snacks: Cold rooms for sweets often use R-404A or R-134a; large stores may use ammonia (not a GHG).

refrigerantLog.why: The defensible way to estimate refrigerant leakage is the mass of refrigerant topped up during the year, from service job sheets or cylinder issue logs, multiplied by its GWP. Without a log the site must fall back on default leak rates, which assessors treat as an estimate.
evidence: AMC service reports with kg charged

contractors.why: Contract workers count in BRSR as 'other than permanent' workers. The BRSR Core safety metrics explicitly include the contract workforce, and wage, minimum-wage, benefits and smaller-town job metrics all include contract labour. Contract labour also triggers licences and registers under the Contract Labour Act / OSH Code.
evidence: Contractor wage registers and PF/ESI challans

sectorNotes.paints: Loading/unloading, tank cleaning, maintenance and housekeeping are commonly contracted.
sectorNotes.snacks: Packing lines often use seasonal contract labour in festive peaks.

headcountSource.why: Person-hours for LTIFR and contract headcount and wages must come from a verifiable record, such as gate-pass or biometric attendance and the contractor's register of workmen, not from estimates. Assessors sample these records.

incidents.why: BRSR needs LTIFR, recordable injuries, high-consequence injuries and fatalities for employees and workers, and BRSR Core adds permanent disabilities and the contract workforce. Only a site-level log that includes contractors and near-misses supports these numbers. Statutory accident notices cover only the more serious cases.

sectorNotes.paints: Paints are a listed hazardous-process industry; include fire/solvent incidents and emergency-plan drills.

permits.why: BRSR P6 E13 asks for a yes/no on environmental compliance and details of every non-compliance, and P1 E2 asks for fines and penalties. Expired consents are a direct non-compliance. Tracking CTE/CTO, hazardous-waste authorisation, groundwater NOC and (for food) FSSAI licence expiry is the control behind a clean 'Yes'.

officeOccupancy.why: Offices are BRSR locations (Section A Q18), and whether they are owned, leased or shared, and how many people use them, decides whether their electricity, water and waste fall in your Scope 1/2 boundary and how shared-building bills are allocated. Large campuses may also be bulk waste generators under the 2026 SWM Rules.
evidence: Floor area and headcount by office

officeBilling.why: Office electricity is Scope 2. Whether it is billed directly by the DISCOM, sub-metered by the landlord, or included in rent (area-based allocation) decides how reliable the kWh figure is. Green-tariff or RE contracts only reduce market-based Scope 2 if they meet the GHG Protocol quality criteria.
evidence: Landlord sub-meter statements or allocation basis

officeHvac.why: Own HVAC means refrigerant leaks (Scope 1 fugitive) and an R-22 phase-out risk. Own DG backup means diesel combustion (Scope 1, energy) and DG stack and noise conditions. If the landlord runs both, they generally fall outside your Scope 1 under operational control and are covered through the lease.
evidence: DG log books and diesel purchases
HVAC AMC service reports with refrigerant top-ups

officeEwaste.why: Laptops, servers, UPS batteries and other IT equipment are BRSR waste category B (and battery waste E). The E-Waste Rules 2022 require bulk consumers to hand e-waste only to registered producers, refurbishers or recyclers, and the handover certificate is both the compliance proof and the evidence of recovery.
evidence: Handover invoices / certificates from CPCB-registered recycler or refurbisher

suggestedQuestions.text: What share of this plant's output (by volume) is solvent-based rather than water-based?
suggestedQuestions.why: Solvent-based production drives VOC emissions, spent-solvent hazardous waste and solvent-storage hazards, while water-based production puts water into the product (consumption) and creates wash water. The split lets esgOS sanity-check air, waste and water figures and supports the 'reduce hazardous chemicals' narrative in P6 E10.

suggestedQuestions.text: Does the CTO set VOC or solvent-related conditions, and how are VOCs quantified?
options: CTO sets VOC limits; monitored by external lab
Solvent mass balance (purchase - product - recovered - waste)
suggestedQuestions.why: BRSR P6 E6 asks for VOC with a unit. A monitored value or a documented mass balance is defensible; a blank is a gap assessors will note.

suggestedQuestions.text: Which hazardous waste categories are on this plant's authorisation?
options: Discarded containers / drums / liners contaminated with hazardous chemicals
suggestedQuestions.why: Each stream must match an authorised Schedule I code and reconcile with Form 3, Form 4 and Form 10 manifests before it is reported as BRSR category G with a recovery or disposal route.

suggestedQuestions.text: For the packaging this plant fills, which plastic EPR categories apply, and who files the brand-owner EPR return?
suggestedQuestions.why: Plastic paint containers create brand-owner EPR obligations (recycling, recycled content) reported in BRSR P2 E4; metal tins do not. Knowing the split per plant lets the company reconcile quantities placed on market.

suggestedQuestions.text: Does this site store hazardous chemicals (e.g., solvents) above MSIHC Rules threshold quantities, i.e., is it a Major Accident Hazard unit?
options: Yes - MAH unit with safety report and on-site emergency plan
Hazardous chemicals stored, below MAH thresholds
suggestedQuestions.why: MAH status brings safety reports, audits and emergency plans that evidence BRSR P3 E10 (hazard identification) and P6 E10, and it flags the site's material risk for Section A Q26.

suggestedQuestions.text: Is the plant zero liquid discharge, and where does process wash water go?
options: ZLD - wash water reused in product / process
ZLD - treated and used for gardening / cooling
suggestedQuestions.why: A ZLD claim in BRSR P6 E5 must agree with zero discharge in E4 and with the CTO. Reusing wash water in water-based batches is a common paint-plant practice that should be documented in the water balance.

suggestedQuestions.text: For TiO2, mica-based pigments and other high-impact raw materials, what supplier data do you hold?
options: Supplier-specific carbon footprint / EPD for TiO2
Responsible-sourcing declaration or audit for mica
Supplier is a value-chain partner >= 2% of purchases
suggestedQuestions.why: Purchased raw materials dominate a paints company's Scope 3 (BRSR P6 Leadership 2). Mica carries child-labour risk relevant to P5 and P2 sourcing. Large suppliers may also be value-chain partners whose BRSR Core data the listed company collects voluntarily from FY2025-26.

suggestedQuestions.text: Which frying oils does this site use, and roughly how many tonnes per year?
suggestedQuestions.why: Edible oil is the largest raw material by value for fried snacks. It drives Scope 3 Category 1 (palm oil also carries land-use risk), the sustainable-sourcing percentage in BRSR P2 E2, and the used-cooking-oil stream.

suggestedQuestions.text: How is used cooking oil handled, and is TPC (total polar compounds) tested?
options: Sold to FSSAI-authorised UCO aggregator (biodiesel); TPC tested
suggestedQuestions.why: FSSAI bars frying with oil above 25% TPC and requires large users (above 50 L/day) to keep records and hand UCO only to authorised collectors. In BRSR it is non-hazardous waste whose route (recovery vs disposal) must be evidenced.

suggestedQuestions.text: Does this site hold a valid FSSAI licence (central or state), and is its expiry tracked alongside the CTE/CTO?
suggestedQuestions.why: The FSSAI licence is a licence to operate for a food plant. Lapses or penalties would surface in BRSR P1 E2, and the licence's product list and capacity should match what esgOS records.

suggestedQuestions.text: Which plastic packaging formats are filled at this site (for EPR)?
options: Multilayer laminates incl. metallised (Category III, confirm)
suggestedQuestions.why: Snack pouches carry brand-owner EPR targets (Category III recycling 30% to 60% between 2024-25 and 2027-28 per secondary sources). Quantities by category, from the packaging bill of materials, feed BRSR P2 E4 and EPR returns.

suggestedQuestions.text: Where do off-spec product, peels and other food waste go?
suggestedQuestions.why: Food waste is BRSR category H (other non-hazardous). Feed, biogas and compost count as recovery; landfill counts as disposal. Large generators may be bulk waste generators under the SWM Rules 2026.

suggestedQuestions.text: Is water used for cleaning / CIP and raw-material washing metered separately, and does effluent pass an oil-and-grease trap or ETP?
suggestedQuestions.why: Cleaning and washing are the biggest water uses in snack plants and return oily effluent. Separate metering supports BRSR water intensity claims, and O&G treatment is needed to meet CTO / Schedule VI limits.

suggestedQuestions.text: Do you run cold rooms or chillers (e.g., for sweets)? Which refrigerant(s)?
suggestedQuestions.why: Refrigerant type sets the GWP of any leak (R-404A ~4,728 vs R-290 0.02 under AR6) and whether it is Scope 1 or reported separately (R-22). It also flags equipment exposed to the R-22 phase-out and HFC phase-down.

suggestedQuestions.text: What is the peak contract/seasonal headcount at this site, and in which months?
suggestedQuestions.why: Peak-season workers are invisible in a 31 March headcount but count in BRSR Core safety (LTIFR including contract workforce), minimum wages, benefits and smaller-town wage metrics. Their person-hours and wages must be captured.
